# Brief shape

Write this and nothing around it. Short enough to read once while walking over.

```markdown
## Who they are
One paragraph. Role, what they actually work on, why that matters in the room
the user is walking into. No childhood, no guessed personality.

## Profiles
- LinkedIn — url, and the headline or latest public line. Or "not found" if that search was empty.
- Instagram — url, and the bio or what the latest public posts are about. Or "not found".
- X — url, and one specific recent post. Or "not found".
- Publications — up to three papers, essays, or talks, each with a link.
- Also — YouTube, personal site, GitHub, only if a page exists.

## Lately
- Up to three specific public things from the last 18 months, each with a link.
- Pull these from the profiles and the publications, not from memory.
- If nothing recent turned up, say so in one line. Do not fill the gap.

## Say this
1. A sentence the user can say out loud. It has to connect the user's angle to a specific post, paper, or profile line.
2. A second, different angle. Not a rephrase of the first.
3. A question that proves they read one specific thing, not "so what are you working on?"

## Don't lead with
One line. Usually the most famous fact, or anything the agents could not pin down.

## If you're not sure
- Name collisions, stale roles, login walls, or claims that had no page behind them.

## Sources
- [title](url)
```

## Voice

- Second person. "You could ask", not "the user might".
- Concrete nouns from the sources: a paper title, a repo, a product, a post.
- If the angle does not intersect their work, say "There isn't a clean bridge" and give the best question anyway. Do not force a fake partnership.

## After they talk

If the user reports what happened, append it under `## After` on the same card.
The next brief may use those lines. It still may not invent anything the user
did not say.
